blocks.heading: Apply social costs and benefits
blocks.text: To apply the concepts, start with a stated decision and distinguish effects on the enterprise from effects on others. An external benefit is a gain to society beyond the business’s own return, such as other users gaining from a shared access improvement funded by a project. An external cost is harm or inconvenience borne by outsiders, such as disruption from deliveries. Describe alternatives and possible mitigation. A benefit elsewhere does not automatically remove a serious harm at the site; the resolution needs a reasoned balance and evidence.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nela Workshop funds an access-road improvement that other residents can also use, while its deliveries add evening noise. The wider access is an external benefit; neighbours’ noise is an external cost. Daytime delivery scheduling may preserve the useful access and business activity while reducing disturbance.

blocks.heading: Social cost
blocks.text: In this syllabus, a social cost is a cost borne by the rest of society rather than the business because of a business decision, also called an external cost. It must identify an outsider’s consequence rather than relabel the firm’s own expenses. Describing the affected people makes the mechanism clear.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Ota Panels’ night deliveries disturb neighbours while the firm pays the carrier. Neighbours’ disturbance is the external cost; paying the carrier is a private business cost.

blocks.heading: Social benefits
blocks.text: Social benefits are the gains to society resulting from a business decision, also known as external benefits in the syllabus. Distinguish wider benefits from the enterprise’s private revenue. Shared infrastructure improvement can benefit other users without becoming their purchase from the firm. Identify who gains and why; do not assume every project provides the same external benefit.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Eya Foods improves shared road access that households also use. Households’ improved access is the wider benefit. Eya’s own extra sales are its private business benefit, a different part of appraisal.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Descriptive social effects and regulation
blocks.text:
Fictional Hena Blocks proposes production near homes. It would create useful output and improve shared road access, but dust would inconvenience residents. Effective maintained dust control is available at a manageable cost. The choice is conditional approval with monitoring or refusing the project.

a(i) Define social cost in the syllabus sense. [2]
a(ii) State two possible environmental-protection measures. [2]
b State two effects on outsiders that could be social costs. [2]
c Explain how a descriptive appraisal should treat Hena’s road benefit and dust harm. [6]
d Evaluate conditional approval against refusal under the stated control facts. [8]

a(i) A business-decision cost borne by the rest of society rather than the business, an external cost. a(ii) Monitored pollution standards and extraction limits. b Noise disturbance and dust-related inconvenience to neighbours. c Shared access can benefit other users while dust imposes a separate cost on residents. Include both alongside private production costs and benefits, examining severity, duration and control rather than treating profit as the whole appraisal. d Effective affordable control can preserve useful output and access while reducing the stated harm. Refusal avoids the project’s disturbance but also forgoes those benefits. Prefer conditional approval with verified maintenance and monitoring here; change the choice if protection proves inadequate rather than assume jobs excuse any harm.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Descriptive social effects and regulation
blocks.text:
Fictional Hena Blocks proposes production near homes. It would create useful output and improve shared road access, but dust would inconvenience residents. Effective maintained dust control is available at a manageable cost. The choice is conditional approval with monitoring or refusing the project.

a Explain how Hena’s decision affects different parties and why its private profit alone cannot resolve the choice. [8]
b Evaluate monitored environmental conditions against refusing the project. [12]

a Owners assess private cost and return, users can gain shared road access and residents bear dust inconvenience. These are different recipients and burdens, so a business profit does not show that residents’ effects have disappeared or been compensated. A descriptive appraisal should examine the effective-control alternative and its ongoing requirements, as well as refusal. b The stated control can reduce harm at manageable cost, making conditional operation a way to retain benefits while protecting neighbours. Monitoring and maintenance use resources and must actually occur; an unenforced promise is insufficient. Refusal offers stronger avoidance of this activity but loses useful output and access. Choose conditions with performance verification under these facts, and restrict or stop activity if the required protection fails. The judgement depends on effective mitigation, not a numerical sum of unmeasured social effects.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Descriptive social effects and regulation
blocks.text:
Fictional Omi Materials proposes a workshop with shared access improvements but noise affecting neighbours. An effective enclosure and daytime schedule can reduce the disturbance at a manageable cost. It compares monitored conditions with refusal. For part (b) only, reliable assessment now shows the proposed controls cannot prevent a severe lasting harm to the nearby community. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate conditional operation at Omi under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate the choice after the assessment of lasting harm changes. Explain whether the original judgement should hold. [12]

a Affordable effective controls can reduce the stated disturbance and preserve shared access and useful activity. Require monitoring and review because a promise alone does not secure performance. Conditional operation is preferable to immediate refusal on the supplied facts. b The essential mitigation condition fails. Severe lasting harm cannot be dismissed because the business or road users gain. Refuse or postpone this proposal while investigating a genuinely safer site or method, rather than repeat ineffective conditions. The recommendation changes because the available protection no longer addresses the harm; keep the assessment descriptive and acknowledge what further evidence is needed.
